newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Wheat up on soybean surge, metals rebound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wheat up on soybean surge, metals rebound.

text.p: Wheat prices rallied sharply on Thursday, in the wake of surging values in the soy complex, on fears potential spring flooding could damage wheat plantings.

Floods in the U.S. Midwest, where the alert has been raised by high soil moisture levels and heavy snow, could flatten some of the winter wheat crop and delay seeding of the spring crop, traders said.
"We still have the threat of flooding this spring," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "There was fund buying and a lack of offers."
And the surge in soybeans, driven by fund-buying and stronger-than-expected U.S. export sales figures, was also a key factor in the wheat rally.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade shot through a psychological level of $4.00 a bushel, and reached a new three-month peak of $4.01 by 1730 GMT.
"Export sales this morning were viewed as very bullish," said a trader in Kansas. "May CBOT beans are up 15 cents and they are dragging up wheat."
However, wheat is still far off its all time high of $7.50, reached a year ago after drought in Russia, Australia and North Africa depressed world grain stocks to their lowest levels for 20 years.
Grain stocks remain low despite a bumper harvest this year.
Overshadowed by grains, base metals still put up a good show on Thursday, shaking off some of the weakness of the last few days to close mostly firmer.
Copper clawed back up on the London Metal Exchange (LME) to close at $2,351.50 per tonne, up $26.50 on the day.
But business was routine, with news Poland's KGHM unions were on strike alert failing to stir the market enough to push prices out of established ranges.
"Copper really is so dull after yesterday," said one trader, referring to Wednesday when copper futures rebounded from a dive to $2,300, lending support to other industrials.
Aluminium also made some gains, mainly on the back of speculative shortcovering, pushing above the $1,650 support level from Wednesday to close at $1,669.
Traders said the market was helped up by output figures for February from the International Primary Aluminium Institute which showed a small fall in daily production.
The only industrial metal close to breaking out of its range was zinc, which extended Wednesday's strong close with a spurt above $1,300 which placed it on the verge of fresh 4-1/2 year highs.
Amongst the precious metals, gold closed firmer, but dipped slightly after U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan made comments signalling interest rates may soon be raised.
Platinum and palladium also finished up on the day.
Disruption to shipping on the Mississippi river sent crude oil prices briefly higher, with benchmark Brent crude hitting a new session high.
May Brent touched $20.42 a barrel before easing back to $20.32 by 1800 GMT.
Marine traffic on the Mississippi river, already hampered by a capsized barge, was closed off to vessels in two other areas.
The United States was also the focus in the coffee market, as London robusta futures followed New York's direction to close mixed.
Robusta May finished the day at $1,655 per tonne - barely changed from Wednesday.

After the London market closed, delegates at an Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) technical meeting in London decided to release more coffee to the market during the first half of 1997.
Prices have shot up this year on tight supplies.
The committee agreed to release 200,000 additional bags of premium arabica coffee exports to the market and withdraw a previous cut of 300,000 tonnes agreed in January.

In January, the ACPC agreed to cut exports by 1.3 million bags -- 1 million bags of the common robusta variety -- so the net effect of Thursday's decision will be a reduction of exports by 800,000 bags.
